items.stem: Describe how mass production changed the car industry in the 1920s.
items.answer: Ford's moving assembly line cut the time to build a Model T to about 90 minutes. The price of a Model T fell to under $300 by the mid-1920s. Car ownership rose rapidly to over 20 million by 1929. The car industry boosted related industries such as steel, rubber, glass and oil. Road building, garages and motels created new jobs.

items.stem: Not all Americans shared in the prosperity of the 1920s. (a) Describe the groups that did not share in the prosperity of the 1920s. [4] (b) Why did farmers not share in the boom? [6]
items.answer: (a) Farmers faced falling prices because of overproduction. Workers in old industries such as coal and textiles faced wage cuts and unemployment. Many African Americans in the South lived in poverty as sharecroppers. Native Americans lived on poor reservation land. Many new immigrants worked in low-paid jobs. (b) Demand from Europe fell after the war. New machinery led to overproduction, so prices fell. Competition from Canada and Argentina. Tariffs led other countries to tax American food exports. Many farmers were in debt from buying land and machinery.

items.stem: ‘The most important reason for the boom of the 1920s was mass production.’ How far do you agree with this statement? Explain your answer.
items.answer: For: It made cars and consumer goods cheap enough for millions. The car industry stimulated steel, rubber, oil and road building. Against: Credit and hire purchase increased demand. Republican policies encouraged business. The First World War had left the USA in a strong economic position. Advertising created new wants. Judgement: Mass production was central, but it depended on credit, advertising and the economic advantages left by the war to create demand.

items.stem: Not all Americans shared in the prosperity of the 1920s. How far did Americans share in the prosperity of the 1920s? Explain your answer.
items.answer: For: Many middle-class families bought cars, radios and electrical goods. Wages rose for many industrial workers. Share ownership spread. Against: Farmers suffered from falling prices. Workers in coal and textiles faced unemployment and wage cuts. Many African Americans and Native Americans remained very poor. Wealth was concentrated among the richest Americans. Judgement: Prosperity was real for the urban middle class but was not shared by large groups, which helps to explain the later crash.

items.stem: (a) Describe the activities of the Ku Klux Klan in the 1920s. [4] (b) Why did intolerance increase in the USA in the 1920s? [6]
items.answer: (a) It attacked African Americans, Jews, Catholics and immigrants. Members wore white robes and burned crosses. It carried out beatings and lynchings. It held mass marches, including in Washington in 1925. It had millions of members and influence in some state governments. (b) Fear of communism after the Russian Revolution led to the Red Scare. Many Americans feared that immigrants threatened jobs and American values. Racism against African Americans was widespread, especially in the South. Religious fundamentalists felt threatened by modern ideas. The Klan exploited these fears.

items.stem: In January 1920 Prohibition banned the manufacture and sale of alcohol in the USA. Describe the problems caused by Prohibition.
items.answer: Speakeasies sold illegal alcohol in their thousands. Bootleggers smuggled alcohol, and moonshine could be poisonous. Organised crime grew, with gangsters such as Al Capone. Police and officials were bribed. Gang violence, such as the St Valentine's Day Massacre in 1929.

items.stem: ‘The 1920s were a time of intolerance rather than freedom in the USA.’ How far do you agree with this statement? Explain your answer.
items.answer: For: The Red Scare and the Sacco and Vanzetti case. The Klan had millions of members. Immigration laws discriminated against southern and eastern Europeans and Asians. The Scopes Trial showed hostility to new ideas. Against: Jazz, cinema and the Harlem Renaissance showed cultural freedom. Some women gained new freedoms. Millions ignored Prohibition. Consumer society gave many more choice. Judgement: The 1920s saw both new freedoms for some urban Americans and strong intolerance towards minorities; for many groups intolerance was the stronger experience.

items.stem: Describe the events of the Wall Street Crash in October 1929.
items.answer: Share prices began to fall in September 1929. On Black Thursday, 24 October, nearly 13 million shares were sold. Bankers tried to support prices by buying shares. On Black Tuesday, 29 October, over 16 million shares were sold and prices collapsed. Many investors, including those who had bought on the margin, were ruined.

items.stem: Describe the effects of the Depression on American people.
items.answer: Unemployment reached about a quarter of the workforce by 1933. Thousands of banks failed and people lost their savings. Many families lost their homes and lived in Hoovervilles. Farmers were evicted when they could not repay debts; the Dust Bowl made things worse. People queued at soup kitchens and travelled the country looking for work.

items.stem: ‘Speculation was the main cause of the Wall Street Crash.’ How far do you agree? Explain your answer.
items.answer: For: Share prices rose far beyond the value of companies. Buying on the margin meant falling prices forced sales and panic. Against: Overproduction meant falling profits, which undermined confidence. Unequal distribution of wealth limited demand. Weak, unregulated banks lent recklessly. Tariffs reduced foreign markets. Judgement: Speculation made the crash so sudden and severe, but the underlying weaknesses of the economy explain why it happened.

items.stem: ‘The New Deal was a success.’ How far do you agree with this statement? Explain your answer.
items.answer: For: It restored confidence in the banks and government. Agencies such as the CCC, PWA and WPA gave work to millions. The TVA transformed a poor region. The Social Security Act created lasting welfare reforms. Against: Unemployment remained high, about 19 per cent in 1938. The 1937 recession showed recovery was fragile. African Americans and women gained less. The AAA helped landowners more than sharecroppers. Judgement: The New Deal succeeded in relief and reform and restored confidence, but it did not achieve full recovery, which came only with war.

Wages rose for many industrial workers. Share ownership spread. Against: Farmers suffered from falling prices. Workers in coal and textiles faced unemployment and wage cuts. Many African Americans and Native Americans remained very poor. Wealth was concentrated among the richest Americans. Judgement: Prosperity was real for the urban middle class but was not shared by large groups, which helps to explain the later crash.

items.stem: What is meant by “Prohibition”?
options: Buying goods by paying in instalments over time.
Roosevelt's programme of relief, recovery and reform to deal with the Depression.
The fear of communists and anarchists in the USA in 1919-20.
The ban on making, selling and transporting alcohol, from 1920 to 1933.
items.answer: The ban on making, selling and transporting alcohol, from 1920 to 1933.

items.stem: Describe the activities of the Ku Klux Klan in the 1920s.
items.answer: It attacked African Americans, Jews, Catholics and immigrants. Members wore white robes and burned crosses. It carried out beatings and lynchings. It held mass marches, including in Washington in 1925. It had millions of members and influence in some state governments.

items.stem: In March 1933 Franklin D. Roosevelt became President of the USA. Why did Roosevelt win the 1932 election? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Hoover was blamed for the Depression. Roosevelt promised a “New Deal” and action to tackle unemployment. He was an energetic, confident campaigner. Hoover's treatment of the Bonus Army damaged him.

items.stem: How important was opposition in limiting the New Deal? Explain your answer.
items.answer: For: The Supreme Court struck down key measures. Business opposition limited reform. The failed court-packing plan of 1937 weakened Roosevelt. Against: Roosevelt won landslide re-elections in 1936 and 1940. The Second New Deal went further despite opposition. Economic limits, such as the 1937 recession, were more important. Judgement: Opposition slowed and shaped the New Deal, but Roosevelt's popularity meant it could not stop it.

items.answer: (a) Accurate. It greatly increased sales of cars and electrical goods. (b) Not accurate. Farmers, workers in old industries, many African Americans and Native Americans did not share in it.

items.stem: What is meant by “speakeasy”?
options: The 1935 law providing old-age pensions and unemployment insurance.
Roosevelt's first hundred days in office in 1933, when many New Deal laws were passed.
An illegal bar selling alcohol during Prohibition.
A tax on imported goods, such as the Fordney-McCumber tariff of 1922.
items.answer: An illegal bar selling alcohol during Prohibition.

items.stem: Describe how the lives of some women changed in the 1920s.
items.answer: Women gained the vote in national elections in 1920. More women worked, for example as secretaries and shop assistants. Flappers wore short skirts and short hair, smoked and danced in public. Labour-saving devices reduced housework for some. Many women, especially in rural areas, saw little change.

items.stem: The New Deal faced strong opposition from both the right and the left. Why did the New Deal face opposition?
items.answer: Businessmen disliked regulation, higher taxes and support for trade unions. Republicans believed it was too costly and un-American. The Supreme Court believed it gave the federal government too much power. Radicals such as Huey Long thought it did too little for the poor. Roosevelt's plan to add judges to the Supreme Court in 1937 alarmed many.
